message.content: I'm sorry you're having chest pain on top of being treated for a blood infection. Let's work out what's going on. Can you describe the pain: where it is, what it feels like (sharp, pressure, tearing), whether it gets worse when you breathe or lie down, and when it started? Also, do you know which germ was found in your blood, and do you have any heart valve problems, an artificial valve, a pacemaker, or a history of injecting drugs?

I'm sorry, doc, I can't really describe it as well as you'd want. Nobody wrote down exactly where it is, what it feels like, or whether breathing or lying down changes it. What I can tell you is that it's new. It started while I've been here in the hospital getting antibiotics through my IV for the blood infection. As for the germ, they told me it's MRSA, the staph that a lot of antibiotics don't work on. They said it has also gotten onto my heart, and they called that endocarditis. I don't have an artificial valve as far as I know. I do have a pacemaker, the small kind with no wires. I've also got a stent in one of the arteries in the front of my heart. I got it for chest pain I used to have, which they called stable angina. I'm also on dialysis because diabetes damaged my kidneys. No one's asked me about drugs before, and nothing about injecting drugs was ever noted.

Thank you, that's very helpful. A blood infection with MRSA that has reached the heart, along with a stent in a heart artery, a leadless pacemaker and dialysis, gives me some important things to look for. Before ordering any tests, I'm going to examine you. I'll listen to your heart and lungs, check for a new murmur or a rubbing sound around the heart, look at your fluid status and your dialysis access, and check for any signs of infected clots elsewhere in your body.

You're going into shock: your heart suddenly isn't pumping well enough. This is an emergency, and the team is starting support for your blood pressure and circulation right now. New chest pain in someone with MRSA infection on a heart valve could have a few causes. A piece of the infection could have broken off and blocked a heart artery, causing a heart attack. The infection could have spread to your coronary stent. An abscess could have formed in the heart wall, or a valve could have suddenly torn. Infected fluid could also have built up around the heart. I'm ordering three tests at once. An ECG (heart tracing) will look for signs of a heart attack. A blood test for troponin will check for heart muscle damage, and other urgent bloods will check how your body is coping. An urgent heart ultrasound (echocardiogram) will look at your valves, the heart wall, how well the heart is pumping, and any fluid around it.

message.content: The heart ultrasound shows two important things. Part of your heart's main pumping chamber has stopped moving properly, which points to a blocked or damaged heart artery. Fluid has also built up around your heart and is now squeezing it, which is called tamponade. In someone with MRSA in the blood and a stent in the front heart artery, I'm most worried that the infection has settled on the stent. That kind of infection can weaken the artery wall into a bulge (a pseudoaneurysm) that can leak or burst into the sac around the heart. The team will need to drain that fluid urgently. I'm also ordering an urgent angiogram, an X-ray dye test of the heart arteries, to look directly at the stent and the artery around it. I'm adding a CT scan of the heart as well, if it can be done safely, to look for an abscess or a bulging artery.

message.content:
Here is what the tests show and what happens next.

The infection in your blood (MRSA) has settled on the stent in the front artery of your heart. It has damaged the stent and weakened the artery wall, which has bulged out into a pocket called a pseudoaneurysm. That pocket is getting bigger quickly. It has leaked into the sac around your heart, which explains your new chest pain. The heart ultrasound showed that part of the heart muscle stopped moving properly. Fluid built up around the heart and squeezed it (tamponade), which caused the shock. The fluid the team drained was cloudy and yellow, which means the sac around your heart is infected as well.

This is a life-threatening emergency. The heart team, which includes heart surgeons, heart specialists and infection specialists, will treat you together:
- **Keeping you stable:** support for your blood pressure and circulation, with a drain left around the heart.
- **Emergency surgery:** most likely to repair or tie off the damaged artery, remove the infected stent and tissue, wash out the sac around the heart, and usually bypass the blocked artery.
- **Antibiotics and tests:** strong IV antibiotics that work against MRSA. The fluid from around your heart will be sent for culture to confirm the germ.
- **Your other conditions:** close planning around your dialysis and a check of your leadless pacemaker for infection.

I know this is a lot to take in. The team will be with you at every step.
